source: Helie, Sun, Xiong (2010) Mixed effects of distractor tasks on incubation (CogSci)
finding: CLARION (implicit bottom level, explicit top level) was used to predict which distractor tasks help incubation. Prediction: a distractor only helps if it does not use the same implicit memory resources as the main task. A human test confirmed it.
numbers: N=114 students, 6 conditions in a free-recall reminiscence task. Condition effect F(5,108)=10.65, p<.001. Do Nothing reminiscence 7.26, higher than all others. No Incubation 4.9, Remote Association 4.84, Perceptual-Motor 4.84. Syllogistic reasoning and dynamic control scored lower than these.
limits: Conference paper. Free recall only. Mixed literature on distractors is explained after the fact by the model. One student sample.
agent_relevance: Older computational system built on an implicit-explicit theory. A pause helps only when the filler step does not load the same resource. For an LLM loop: an idle gap does nothing by itself, since a model has no hidden process between calls.

source: Helie and Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psychological Review)
finding: Explicit-Implicit Interaction (EII) theory has five principles: explicit and implicit knowledge coexist and differ; both are active in most tasks; representations are redundant; results are integrated; processing is iterative and may be bidirectional. CLARION simulations captured incubation (free recall, lexical decision) and insight/overshadowing effects.
numbers: Search snippets and press only; no figures read. Press says model output was nearly identical to earlier human data (e.g. the coin question).
limits: Not opened. Numbers must be taken from the original paper before use. Fits to older human data, not new predictions.
agent_relevance: The source of the loop: explicit try, implicit association pool, integrate, check, repeat. Our schema already has the check; the implicit pool maps to many cheap diverse samples.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: Are large language models creative problem solvers? (NAACL)
finding: On about 1,600 everyday-innovation problems, humans and LLMs fail differently. Humans solve or fail completely. GPT-4 is middling and often proposes physically impossible steps. Two scaffolds from creativity theory helped: step-wise self-reflection and divergent-convergent thinking.
numbers: Majority-vote humans 79.3% correct vs GPT-4 73.3%. Dataset 78% solvable, 22% unsolvable. Largest error: wrong tool use 42.4% of errors; goal not reached 17.7%; unfaithful to constraints 16.9% plus 9.5%. 180 solvable problems for prompts. GPT-4: self-reflect cut infeasible solutions 9.7% (div-conv 4.3%); div-conv raised efficient solutions 6.5% (self-reflect 2.2%). Claude2 and Llama2-13b gained from div-conv but not from self-reflect.
limits: Small prompt-test set. Gains are a few points. Smaller models cannot self-reflect on physical consequences.
agent_relevance: Direct use of a spontaneous-then-controlled split inside a prompt scaffold. Small but real gain; the divergent step helps efficiency, the check step helps feasibility. Supports engineering variation then a code or world check.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2024/2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Tested the implicit-explicit split on LLMs using human tasks where verbal thinking hurts (Fallshore and Schooler 1993 artificial grammar; face recognition; learning with exceptions, Williams and Lombrozo). Chain of thought (CoT) cut accuracy in several of them.
numbers: Artificial grammar (50% chance): o1-preview vs GPT-4o zero-shot on 440 problems, drop 36.3 points (94.0% to 57.7%). GPT-4o full set 87.5% to 64.4% (-23.1). Claude 3 Opus -8.0, Gemini 1.5 Pro -6.05, Llama 3.1 70B -8.8, Claude 3.5 Sonnet +1.8 (no drop). Face recognition (20% chance): GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2; Claude 3 Opus 44.0 to 29.6; Gemini 54.6 from 66.0; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 to 94.8. Exceptions task: GPT-4o needed 12.5 passes vs 2.9 (+331%); Claude 3.5 Sonnet 6.4 vs 2.3; Claude 3 Opus 5.5 vs 2.4. GPT-4o with CoT stalled near 80%. Three other tasks mixed.
limits: Only three of six tasks showed clear harm. Steering prompts and tree-of-thought only partly repaired it. o1 could not be run without its built-in reasoning.
agent_relevance: Strongest machine evidence that explicit verbal reasoning can hurt where the pattern is statistical. Our schema should not force a written rationale on perceptual, pattern or exception-heavy items; try a no-rationale arm and compare.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI delivers creative output but struggles with thinking processes
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4 and GPT-4o beat students on divergent, convergent and verbal insight tasks, but lost on creative writing and on process measures such as forward flow and representational change. The authors say the output comes from non-creative mechanisms.
numbers: Exp1 AUT: 100 humans vs 100 instances per model; model novelty higher (t=5.32, 5.10, 8.89, all p<.001); appropriateness lower for GPT-3.5 (t=-3.37) and GPT-4 (t=-4.60), no difference for GPT-4o (p=.163). Exp2 RAT: 61 humans; GPT-4o accuracy 0.35 above humans, GPT-4 0.26, GPT-3.5 0.19. Temperature 0.6-0.8, penalties 1.
limits: Chinese students, one language mix, API settings fixed to prior work. Process measures rely on embeddings. Preregistered.
agent_relevance: Models are strong on output measures yet differ in process. Do not infer human-like ordinary processes from good output; measure our own process traces.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Exps 3 and 5 (insight, association)
finding: Insight results were mixed by model and task. Humans moved farther from the prompt in free and chain association than most models, so model association chains were closer and more redundant.
numbers: Chinese character puzzle: humans above GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (+0.09 each) but below GPT-4o (-0.21). Stumpers: humans above GPT-3.5 (+0.20) and GPT-4 (+0.06), below GPT-4o (-0.06, p=.011). Rebus: GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o above humans by 0.32 and 0.39. Free association distance: humans higher than GPT-3.5 (t=15.15), GPT-4 (t=6.14), GPT-4o (t=17.39). Forward flow: humans higher than GPT-3.5 (t=7.46), GPT-4 (t=3.59, p=.003), GPT-4o (t=9.94); in chain association not different from GPT-4o (p=.150).
limits: 60 humans per insight task. Rebus only for models with image input.
agent_relevance: Model association drifts less far from the start. Engineered variation (distant seeds, forced diversity) is needed because a plain sample stays near the cue.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Exps 6 to 8 (representational change, evaluation, selection)
finding: On a task needing a new problem representation, humans beat the models and used transformation. The models used logical reasoning and did well on neither representation change nor picking the most creative idea.
numbers: Representational change (24 problems, 4 options): humans above GPT-4-turbo by 0.46 and GPT-4o by 0.31 (p<.001). Strategy: GPT-4o 68.88% and GPT-4-turbo 71.26% reasoning; humans 72.41% transformation. Creative selection: higher decision error in models (abstract). No link between novelty and appropriateness weights in models.
limits: Only GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o (image input). Strategy coded by raters from self-reports, alpha .88.
agent_relevance: Weak point is restructuring, which we also target with reframing (O-operators). A reframing step should be forced from a code signal, not left to the model's natural reasoning style.

source: Chen and Ding (2023) Probing the creativity of large language models: can models produce divergent semantic association? (Findings of EMNLP)
finding: On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), GPT-4 with greedy decoding beat 96% of humans and GPT-3.5-turbo beat the human average. Sampling and higher temperature helped weaker models but made them unstable. GPT-4 did not gain from them.
numbers: GPT-4 greedy DAT 89.1, above 96.1% of humans. GPT-3.5-turbo 80.8, above average human. Other models roughly proportional to size. Top-p 0.9 with temperature 0.7; temperature varied 0.1 to 1. Surprisal control: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 still above human average, GPT-4 margin smaller.
limits: DAT measures word distance only. Words can be rare rather than creative. Weak link to real tasks.
agent_relevance: Temperature is a cheap variation lever for mid models but unstable. Strong models do better by prompt or structure than by noise.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We are different, we are the same: creative homogeneity across LLMs
finding: LLMs match or beat humans on individual creativity tests (AUT, forward flow, DAT) yet their answers are far more similar to one another than human answers are. A creativity-prompting system message raised individual scores and variability only slightly.
numbers: 22 LLMs in the first analysis; family-controlled subset used later. Human sample N=102 (Prolific). Population variability lower for LLMs on all tests (t-tests significant for all three tests). Creative system prompts raised LLM originality a little (e.g. AUT scores 0.733 'more creative', 0.754 'very creative', 0.702 'not creative'). Humans still more variable. One-word-answer control keeps the result.
limits: Online human sample scores lower than earlier studies. Embedding similarity is a proxy.
agent_relevance: Samples from different models are not independent in creative output either (matches G4). More samples from one or more models will not give true variation; force diversity through structure.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: An agent that overgenerates thousands of ideas, removes duplicates and ranks them produced ideas judged more novel than expert ideas but slightly less feasible. Variation plus selection works; the LLM ranker is not a reliable judge.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition. Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p<.05 after correction). Feasibility coefficient for AI -0.330. 79 reviewers, 298 unique reviews. 4000 seed ideas per topic; dedup at similarity 0.8 left about 5% non-duplicates (about 200). LLM ranker with pairwise rounds N=5; accuracy on accept/reject about 71.4% (Claude-3.5-Sonnet).
limits: Novelty judged without running the ideas. Reviewers may over-weight novelty. LLM self-evaluation failed.
agent_relevance: Best direct test of engineering variation at scale. Diversity plateaus fast, so mass sampling needs dedup and an outside check. Supports the honing idea of generate wide, select with a non-model signal.

source: Liu, Dubova, Conklin, Harada, Griffiths (2026) Assessing the effect of cross-domain mapping on creativity in humans and LLMs
finding: Remote cross-domain prompts raised human originality but gave LLMs no average benefit. Only the two top models gained, and only for distant sources. Humans transferred surface features; models transferred structure and function.
numbers: 140 humans and 7 LLMs, 100 target-source pairs, 2,800 ideas, 1,002 raters. Originality (1-5): human cross-domain 2.93, human user-need 2.57, o3 3.83, Claude-Sonnet-4 3.76, Llama-3.3-70b 3.02. Condition effect b=0.36 (p<.001); source by condition b=0.48. Distant 50% of pairs b=0.12 (p=.029); distant 10% b=0.24 (p=.024). Semantic distance predicted originality, human beta .10, LLM beta .18.
limits: Product-design task; o3 used to normalize wording. Overlaps with analogy subfield.
agent_relevance: A mechanism that helps people (random remote cue) may do nothing for a model. Test each variation operator on our agent; do not assume transfer from human findings.

source: Nath, Dayan, Stevenson (2024) Characterising the creative process in humans and large language models
finding: Human AUT answers follow two routes: deep search in few semantic spaces, or flexible broad search; both reach similar creativity. LLMs lean to one route by task, and more flexible models score higher on creativity.
numbers: Abstract page only; no numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract read; models and statistics not read.
agent_relevance: Ordinary-process claim: creativity comes from exploring semantic space with common moves. Jump profiles are a usable process trace for our agent.

source: Domanti, Campidelli, Agnoli, De Angeli (2026) Are semantic networks associated with idea originality in artificial creativity?
finding: ChatGPT-4o produced far more words and responses but its semantic network was more rigid and fragmented than both human groups, while its originality was above low-creative humans and below high-creative humans. The human link between flexible networks and originality did not appear for the model.
numbers: 81 students vs 81 ChatGPT-4o runs. Fluency GPT 43.8, high-creative 19.1, low 12.2 (F(2,159)=438, eta2=.846). Average shortest path: GPT 4.378, low 3.429, high 3.325. Modularity: GPT 0.692, low 0.666, high 0.662. Resilience: GPT 77.9 vs 85.2 and 85.8 (d about 4). Originality peaks: GPT vs high-creative B=-0.34, vs low B=+0.24 (p<.001).
limits: One model, chat interface, no hyperparameters, correlational, median split, possible training leak of AUT.
agent_relevance: Associative-network accounts of ordinary creativity do not predict model originality. Output novelty in LLMs can come from breadth of production, not flexible structure, which supports mass variation plus a filter.

source: Ismayilzada et al. (2026) Large language models align with the human brain during creative thinking
finding: Model representations align with default-mode-network activity during the human Alternate Uses Task, more for bigger models and better creative scorers, but mostly at the prompt stage rather than in generated text. A creativity-optimized post-training kept alignment for high-creativity responses; reasoning distillation reversed it.
numbers: Open models 270M to 72B. DMN alignment vs size r=0.58, vs AUT score r=0.51 (both p<0.05); best layer depth r=0.54. 1,358 high and 1,978 low creativity responses; four raters ICC=0.75. Sampling temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95. Reasoning-distilled Llama-8B: negative alignment for high-creative responses.
limits: Modest number of models; sample size of human fMRI unclear (170 stated, 88 removed); frontoparietal result only partly replicated.
agent_relevance: Hints that reasoning-style tuning moves a model away from the creative (default-mode-like) pattern. Matches c04: more explicit reasoning is not free for creative or implicit work.

source: Nobrega Medeiros (2026) TACIT: transformation-aware capturing of implicit thought
finding: A diffusion model that maps maze problem to solution in pixel space shows a sudden jump: the solution is invisible for 68% of the process, then appears across the whole path in 2%. The author compares this to eureka moments.
numbers: Trained on 1 million synthetic mazes; 192x training-loss reduction; final IoU 99.6% (one table value 97.1%); 96.9% IoU at fewer steps.
limits: Single independent author, preprint, one toy domain, no human data. The insight link is an analogy only.
agent_relevance: A computational implicit-process model, but tied to images and not to our text loop. Weak evidence; do not use for design.

source: Anonymous authors (2024) Creative problem solving in large language and vision models: what would it take? (2024)
finding: Appendix B argues EII theory (Helie and Sun 2010) can map onto ML: preparation to problem formulation, incubation and illumination to knowledge representation and manipulation, verification to evaluation. No LLM test of EII is given. Also notes the one direct use of divergent-convergent prompting is MacGyver.
numbers: Vision-language test of object replacement: CLIP-B-32 100.0%, B-16 92.0%, L-14 98.0%, H-14 98.0%, ViLT 68.0% accuracy without creativity (about 30% chance for random pick).
limits: Position paper; the EII mapping is untested.
agent_relevance: Confirms there is no direct LLM test of EII yet. A clean experiment is open: compare a plain loop with one that has separate wide-sampling and check stages.

source: Gabora (2017) Honing theory: a complex systems framework for creativity (Nonlinear Dynamics, Psychology, and Life Sciences)
finding: Honing theory: creative work is a mind reducing internal conflict and entropy by iteratively reshaping an idea (half-baked, then honed) in response to context. It links to contextual focus, shifting between associative and analytic modes.
numbers: Theory paper; no experiment numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Hard to falsify. Little direct human or LLM test.
agent_relevance: Frames iteration as repeated refinement under changing context, which is what our loop already does. Treat as a design story, not evidence.

source: Polyak and Balkhyoor (2026) Before the prompt: heteromorphic imagination and the cognitive cost of premature crystallization in human-AI co-creativity (ICCC)
finding: Argues that a text prompt forces an idea into words before it is ready (premature crystallization), and connects this to honing theory and contextual focus. A theory paper, no experiment.
numbers: No quantitative results.
limits: Conceptual; no data. Applies to human-AI co-creation, not to autonomous agents.
agent_relevance: Warns that forcing early verbal commitment may harm half-formed ideas. For an agent, delay the commitment step until after wide variation; weak support only.

source: Franceschelli and Musolesi (2026) On the creativity of AI agents
finding: Separates functionalist creativity (outputs) from ontological creativity (process, press, producer). Says LLM agents show some functional creativity but lack intrinsic motivation, continual learning and intentionality. Notes outputs collapse into generic text without a specific originality prompt.
numbers: No quantitative results.
limits: Conceptual.
agent_relevance: Fits an ordinary-process view only for outputs. We aim at functional creativity, so process arguments need not block the design.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind your step, steering and tree-of-thought appendices
finding: The arXiv text states that reasoning does not simply remove the harm: in the artificial grammar task o1-preview stays far below GPT-4o zero-shot (57.7% vs 94.0%), and stricter steering toward the right strategy only partly closed gaps.
numbers: Zero-shot GPT-4o subset 94.00%. o1-preview 57.70%. Llama 3 8B 59.7 to 57.9; Llama 3 70B 60.5 to 58.3. Logical inconsistency task (opposite sign): GPT-4o rose from 53.2 to 93.9% (MNLI) with CoT; Llama 3.1 70B 55.6 to 81.6; Claude 3 Opus fell 62.7 to 58.8.
limits: Logical-inconsistency task is where CoT helps; shows effect is task-type dependent.
agent_relevance: Task-type switch needed: explicit reasoning for logic-type items, direct answering for pattern-type items. Choose by task class or by a measured pilot, not by habit.

source: Orwig et al. (2024) The language of creativity: evidence from humans and large language models (J Creative Behavior); cited in Zhang et al. 2025
finding: Cited in the opened Zhang paper: GPT-4 stories on the five-sentence task were significantly less creative than human stories. Zhang also cites expert-writer comparisons (Marco et al. 2024) where GPT-4 was worse.
numbers: No numbers read in this session; only as cited text.
limits: Second-hand. Open the original before using.
agent_relevance: Creative writing is a place where plain sampling underperforms; an extended loop may be needed.

source: Orru et al. (2023) and Raz et al. (2024) GPT-3 and GPT-4 on verbal insight tasks; cited in Zhang et al. 2025
finding: Cited in the opened Zhang paper: GPT-3 performed comparably to humans on verbal insight tasks; GPT-4 significantly outperformed humans on similar tasks (stumpers).
numbers: No numbers read in this session; only as cited text.
limits: Second-hand. Verbal insight puzzles are likely well covered in training data.
agent_relevance: Insight puzzle success alone does not show restructuring ability (see c07).

source: Fallshore and Schooler (1993) Verbal vs. nonverbal processing in artificial grammar learning; Williams and Lombrozo (2013); both tested on LLMs in Liu et al. 2025
finding: Original human results that Liu et al. adapted: people asked to verbalize do worse at artificial grammar judgments, and people asked to explain learn data with exceptions more slowly.
numbers: Original human numbers not read; LLM replication is in c04.
limits: Second-hand through the LLM paper. Human replication status of verbal overshadowing is mixed (not checked this session).
agent_relevance: Gives the human anchor for the LLM result in c04. Check the replication record before leaning on it.

source: Doshi and Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content (Science Advances)
finding: Writers with AI ideas wrote stories judged more creative, but stories became more similar to each other. Same direction as Wenger and Kenett.
numbers: Not opened; figures not recorded.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Individual gain with collective sameness; one agent with many samples shares this risk.

source: Hubert, Awa, Zabelina (2024) The current state of artificial intelligence generative language models is more creative than humans on divergent thinking tasks (Scientific Reports); Koivisto and Grassini (2023)
finding: Cited in Zhang: matched-count AUT comparison where chatbots scored higher than humans on divergent thinking. Zhang followed the same 1:1 response-count matching.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Output-level creativity of chat models on AUT is well established; process-level evidence (c05 to c07, c13) is where models differ.

source: Du, Gordon, Tolmie (2025) Role of mind wandering during incubation in divergent and convergent thinking (Brain Sciences); McDaniel, Habibi, Kaplan (2025, Scientific Reports)
finding: Search-result summaries: mind wandering during incubation did not predict divergent thinking and its effect on convergent thinking was context dependent (Du et al.). A preregistered writing study found mind wandering predicted gains (McDaniel et al.). No LLM study of incubation or mind wandering was found in a targeted search.
numbers: Not opened; none recorded.
limits: Search snippets only.
agent_relevance: Human incubation evidence is mixed, and no LLM incubation test was found. Gap: a controlled test of an inserted unrelated step in an LLM loop has not been reported.
